Title: AdaCtrl: Towards Adaptive and Controllable Reasoning via Difficulty-Aware Budgeting
Authors: Shijue Huang, Hongru Wang, Wanjun Zhong, Zhaochen Su, Jiazhan Feng, Bowen Cao, Yi R. Fung
Research Question: How to dynamically allocate reasoning token budget based on self-assessed difficulty while giving users budget controllability?
Main Method: Two-stage training: Cold-start SFT for difficulty self-assessment and budget tagging, followed by difficulty-aware RL with length-calibrated reward.
Model Assumptions: Requires fine-tuning/RL of reasoning model weights; assumes discrete difficulty tiers.
Baselines: Standard CoT, fixed-length RL baselines, vanilla SFT
Evaluation Metrics: Token reduction percentage, task accuracy, length compliance
Main Reported Findings: Reduces reasoning length by 62-91% on simple datasets and >10% on hard ones while maintaining accuracy.
Stated Limitations: Does not support abstention; requires expensive RL post-training.
Relationship to ThinkOrQuit: AdaCtrl addresses difficulty-aware budgeting but forces an answer even when uncertain. ThinkOrQuit adds selective abstention without weight retraining.
Potential Overlap: Shared motivation of difficulty budgeting, but AdaCtrl requires RL training and does not abstain.

Title: Conformal Thinking: Risk Control for Reasoning on a Compute Budget
Authors: Xi Wang, Anushri Suresh, Alvin Zhang, Rishi More, William Jurayj, Benjamin Van Durme, Mehrdad Farajtabar, Daniel Khashabi, Eric Nalisnick
Research Question: How to set adaptive reasoning token budgets to guarantee a user-specified risk level while minimizing compute?
Main Method: Distribution-free risk control using dual thresholds: upper threshold (stop when confident) and parametric lower threshold (preemptively stop unsolvable instances).
Model Assumptions: Exchangeability between calibration and test distributions; access to validation set for quantile calibration.
Datasets / Benchmarks: GSM8K, MATH, reasoning benchmarks across diverse models
Baselines: Fixed token budget, greedy decoding, single-threshold conformal prediction
Evaluation Metrics: Error rate (selective risk), compute cost (tokens), coverage
Main Reported Findings: Dual thresholds reduce reasoning compute while strictly adhering to user-specified error risk targets on i.i.d. validation/test splits.
Stated Limitations: Guarantees collapse under distribution shift; requires separate lower-threshold calibration for unsolvability.
Relationship to ThinkOrQuit: Directly inspires the dual-threshold risk-control framing in ThinkOrQuit, but ThinkOrQuit investigates robustness under shift and limited calibration data.
Potential Overlap: High theoretical overlap in budget-as-risk-control; ThinkOrQuit must distinguish itself by focusing on distribution shift, small calibration data, and explicit tri-action policy.

Title: Knowing When to Quit: A Principled Framework for Dynamic Abstention in LLM Reasoning
Authors: Hen Davidov, Nachshon Cohen, Oren Kalinsky, Yaron Fairstein, Guy Kushilevitz, Ram Yazdi, Patrick Rebeschini
Research Question: Can an LLM dynamically quit mid-generation when reasoning is unpromising to maximize selective accuracy?
Main Method: Dynamic mid-generation abstention modeled as regularized RL; derives value function approximation to trigger quit action when value falls below threshold.
Model Assumptions: Markov decision process assumption; requires value network or policy training.
Datasets / Benchmarks: Mathematical reasoning benchmarks, toxicity avoidance tasks
Baselines: Pre-generation abstention, post-generation abstention, fixed-threshold baselines
Evaluation Metrics: Selective accuracy, abstention rate, average token cost
Main Reported Findings: Dynamic mid-generation quitting outperforms static pre/post abstention on selective accuracy while cutting token cost.
Stated Limitations: Requires RL training or value function approximation; not designed for training-free offline inference-time policies.
Relationship to ThinkOrQuit: Demonstrates that mid-generation quitting is superior to static abstention. ThinkOrQuit builds a lightweight, inference-time counterpart without full RL.
Potential Overlap: Overlap in dynamic abstention concept; ThinkOrQuit avoids RL training, focusing on offline trace-based lightweight policies.

Title: R-Tuning: Instructing Large Language Models to Say "I Don't Know"
Authors: Hanning Zhang, Shizhe Diao, Yong Lin, Yi R. Fung, Qing Lian, Xingyao Wang, Yangyi Chen, Heng Ji, Tong Zhang
Research Question: Can LLMs be trained to recognize parametric knowledge boundaries and refuse unknown questions?
Main Method: Refusal-aware instruction tuning: labels questions as answerable/unanswerable based on model knowledge and trains refusal behavior.
Model Assumptions: Requires instruction fine-tuning on identified knowledge boundaries.
Baselines: Standard instruction tuning, vanilla prompting, Few-Shot prompting
Evaluation Metrics: Selective accuracy, rejection precision/recall, expected calibration error
Main Reported Findings: R-Tuning significantly improves refusal accuracy on unknown questions and generalizes across out-of-domain tasks.
Stated Limitations: Static pre-generation refusal; does not perform adaptive reasoning or test-time computation allocation.
Relationship to ThinkOrQuit: Provides foundational evidence that abstention generalizes, but ThinkOrQuit acts dynamically during reasoning rather than via static SFT.
Potential Overlap: No overlap in test-time compute allocation; complementary concept of refusal.

Title: AbstentionBench: Reasoning LLMs Fail on Unanswerable Questions
Authors: Polina Kirichenko, Mark Ibrahim, Kamalika Chaudhuri, Samuel J. Bell
Research Question: How well do modern LLMs (including reasoning models) abstain across diverse failure modes?
Main Method: Comprehensive benchmark comprising 20 datasets across 6 abstention categories (unanswerable, underspecified, stale data, etc.) with validated judges.
Model Assumptions: Black-box model inference; evaluates standard generation and reasoning prompting.
Datasets / Benchmarks: 20 datasets across 6 scenarios (unanswerable math, ambiguous questions, false premise, etc.)
Baselines: Direct answering, few-shot prompting across 20 open and closed models
Evaluation Metrics: Abstention precision, recall, F1, accuracy under selective prediction
Main Reported Findings: Reasoning models overthink and fail catastrophically on unanswerable questions, exhibiting extreme overconfidence.
Stated Limitations: Benchmark paper; does not propose an inference-time dynamic control algorithm.
Relationship to ThinkOrQuit: Provides the empirical motivation for ThinkOrQuit: test-time reasoning models urgently require abstention mechanisms.
Potential Overlap: No algorithmic overlap; serves as motivation and potential shifted evaluation benchmark.

Title: Dynamic Early Exit in Reasoning Models
Authors: Chenxu Yang, Qingyi Si, Yongjie Duan, Zheliang Zhu, Chenyu Zhu, Qiaowei Li, Zheng Lin, Li Cao, Weiping Wang
Research Question: Can reasoning models self-truncate Chain-of-Thought sequences early without retraining?
Main Method: Monitors model confidence at reasoning transition points and exits early when high confidence in a trial answer is reached.
Model Assumptions: Training-free; assumes access to intermediate checkpoint answer extractions and confidence scores.
Datasets / Benchmarks: GSM8K, MATH-500, GPQA, AIME across 11 models
Baselines: Full CoT, fixed-length truncation, random early exit
Main Reported Findings: Dynamic early exit reduces tokens by up to 80% and actually improves accuracy by 0.3-5.0% by eliminating overthinking.
Stated Limitations: Only considers early stopping when confident; does not handle abstention for unsolvable queries.
Relationship to ThinkOrQuit: Represents the 'Answer early' arm of ThinkOrQuit. ThinkOrQuit unifies early exit with 'Quit/Abstain'.
Potential Overlap: Overlap in confidence-based early exit; ThinkOrQuit extends this to a tri-action decision space including abstention.

Title: Rational Metareasoning for Large Language Models
Authors: C. Nicolo De Sabbata, Theodore R. Sumers, Thomas L. Griffiths
Research Question: Can LLMs optimize intermediate reasoning steps using cognitive models of the Value of Computation?
Main Method: Formulates a reward function incorporating the Value of Computation (penalizing reasoning steps) and trains models via Expert Iteration.
Model Assumptions: Requires Expert Iteration fine-tuning and task reward definition.
Baselines: Few-shot CoT, STaR, standard prompt baselines
Evaluation Metrics: Task accuracy, total token cost, Pareto efficiency frontier
Main Reported Findings: Reduces reasoning token count by 20-37% while matching full CoT accuracy.
Stated Limitations: Requires iterative training cycles; does not address selective prediction or abstention.
Relationship to ThinkOrQuit: Provides theoretical grounding for the Value-of-Computation objective in ThinkOrQuit.
Potential Overlap: Conceptual overlap in Value-of-Computation framing; ThinkOrQuit applies it at inference-time without model training.

Title: Mitigating LLM Hallucinations via Conformal Abstention
Authors: Yasin Abbasi-Yadkori, Ilja Kuzborskij, David Stutz, Andras Gyorgy, Adam Fisch, Arnaud Doucet, Iuliya Beloshapka, Wei-Hung Weng, Yao-Yuan Yang, Csaba Szepesvari, Ali Taylan Cemgil, Nenad Tomasev
Research Question: Can conformal prediction guarantee controlled hallucination rates via self-consistency abstention?
Main Method: Applies Conformal Risk Control using self-consistency agreement as a non-conformity score to set an abstention threshold with finite-sample guarantees.
Model Assumptions: Exchangeability between calibration and test data; fixed number of generated candidate responses.
Baselines: Standard greedy generation, raw self-consistency thresholding
Evaluation Metrics: Selective accuracy, coverage, empirical error rate, bound violation rate
Main Reported Findings: Conformal abstention guarantees error control within specified alpha while maximizing coverage.
Stated Limitations: Fixed inference compute budget per problem; does not dynamically vary reasoning token depth.
Relationship to ThinkOrQuit: Provides the statistical foundation for risk control via consistency. ThinkOrQuit couples this with adaptive reasoning budgets.
Potential Overlap: Overlap in conformal calibration of consistency; ThinkOrQuit applies this to dynamic multi-step reasoning traces.

Title: Domain-Shift-Aware Conformal Prediction for Large Language Models
Authors: Zhexiao Lin, Yuanyuan Li, Neeraj Sarna, Yuanyuan Gao, Michael von Gablenz
Research Question: How can conformal prediction guarantees be maintained for LLMs under domain shift?
Main Method: Reweights calibration samples based on semantic embedding similarity between calibration prompts and test prompts (DS-CP).
Model Assumptions: Access to prompt embeddings; bounded likelihood ratio between source and target domains.
Baselines: Standard split conformal prediction, unweighted CP
Evaluation Metrics: Marginal coverage, conditional coverage, prediction set size
Main Reported Findings: DS-CP preserves target coverage guarantees under severe domain shifts where standard CP exhibits significant under-coverage.
Stated Limitations: Evaluated on classification/multiple-choice tasks; does not evaluate multi-step reasoning or dynamic compute budgets.
Relationship to ThinkOrQuit: Highlights the critical vulnerability of naive conformal prediction under distribution shift, motivating ThinkOrQuit's shift-aware evaluation.
Potential Overlap: Methodological contrast: DS-CP uses sample reweighting for static sets; ThinkOrQuit tests how policy thresholds degrade under shift in reasoning.

Title: CaTS: Calibrated Test-Time Scaling for Efficient LLM Reasoning
Authors: Chengsong Huang, Langlin Huang, Jixuan Leng, Jiacheng Liu, Jiaxin Huang
Research Question: How can multi-sample test-time scaling be calibrated to stop sampling early when answers are confident?
Main Method: Calibrated test-time scaling with early stopping (CaTS-ES) and confidence-weighted self-consistency (CaTS-SC).
Model Assumptions: Access to model log-probabilities or verbalized confidences across sampled reasoning paths.
Evaluation Metrics: Accuracy, sample efficiency (average number of samples N), ECE
Main Reported Findings: CaTS-ES saves 40-70% of sampled paths while maintaining or improving self-consistency accuracy.
Stated Limitations: Focuses on sample count stopping; does not include an explicit 'abstain' mechanism when samples disagree or difficulty is insurmountable.
Relationship to ThinkOrQuit: Direct baseline for adaptive compute stopping. ThinkOrQuit adds selective abstention to prevent forced errors on high disagreement.
Potential Overlap: Overlap in confidence-based stopping of test-time scaling; ThinkOrQuit evaluates tri-action decision space.

Title: Online Reasoning Calibration: Test-Time Training Enables Generalizable Conformal LLM Reasoning
Research Question: Can test-time training enable valid conformal risk bounds for reasoning models under reasoning distribution shift?
Main Method: ORCA: Combines conformal prediction with test-time training (TTT) probes updated per input to maintain valid confidence under reasoning shift.
Model Assumptions: Requires test-time gradient updates or specialized probe architecture.
Datasets / Benchmarks: Complex mathematical reasoning, out-of-distribution reasoning benchmarks
Baselines: Static conformal prediction, uncalibrated reasoning scaling
Evaluation Metrics: Empirical risk, token efficiency, coverage error under shift
Main Reported Findings: Demonstrates that reasoning pattern shifts invalidate static conformal bounds, and per-input adaptation restores validity.
Stated Limitations: High compute overhead of test-time training probes; unsuitable for lightweight deployment.
Relationship to ThinkOrQuit: Confirms the hypothesis that distribution shift degrades reasoning calibration; ThinkOrQuit investigates whether lightweight inference policies can detect shift without heavy TTT.
Potential Overlap: Thematic overlap in conformal reasoning calibration under shift; ThinkOrQuit focuses on lightweight, non-gradient policies.

Title: Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
Authors: Charlie Snell, Jaehoon Lee, Kelvin Xu, Aviral Kumar
Research Question: How does test-time compute scale relative to pre-training compute, and how should it be allocated across difficulty?
Main Method: Analyzes compute-optimal test-time scaling via search, verifiers (PRMs), and difficulty-aware compute allocation.
Model Assumptions: Access to verifiers / reward models; problem difficulty estimation.
Baselines: Fixed compute per problem, greedy decoding, Best-of-N without verifier
Main Reported Findings: Compute-optimal test-time scaling can outperform a 14x larger model trained with standard compute on mathematical reasoning.
Stated Limitations: Assumes verifier is available and well-calibrated; does not address selective abstention.
Relationship to ThinkOrQuit: Foundational empirical basis for test-time compute allocation based on difficulty.

Title: Selective Classification for Deep Neural Networks
Research Question: How to formalize risk-coverage trade-offs and construct optimal selective classifiers with guaranteed risk?
Main Method: Selective classifier framework using confidence selection function g(x) >= theta; defines selective risk and coverage, proving empirical risk bounds.
Main Reported Findings: Guarantees selective risk control under confidence thresholding on i.i.d. validation data.
Stated Limitations: Formulated for classification, not generative multi-step reasoning.
Relationship to ThinkOrQuit: Provides the exact mathematical formulation of selective risk, coverage, and RC-AUC used in ThinkOrQuit.
Potential Overlap: Foundational theoretical framework adopted by ThinkOrQuit.

Title: Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models
Authors: Xuezhi Wang, Jason Wei, Dale Schuurmans, Quoc Le, Ed Chi, Sharan Narang, Aakanksha Chowdhery, Denny Zhou
Research Question: Does sampling diverse reasoning paths and taking majority vote improve reasoning accuracy and calibrate confidence?
Main Method: Sample diverse reasoning paths via temperature sampling and aggregate final answers via majority voting.
Main Reported Findings: Self-consistency improves accuracy by 10-20% across math and logic benchmarks; majority margin correlates strongly with accuracy.
Stated Limitations: Infers a fixed, high compute cost (e.g. N=40 paths) uniformly across all problems.
Relationship to ThinkOrQuit: Self-consistency margin serves as the foundational confidence feature in ThinkOrQuit.
Potential Overlap: Core baseline and feature source for adaptive stopping and abstention.

Title: Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? An Empirical Evaluation of Confidence Elicitation in LLMs
Authors: Miao Xiong, Zhiyuan Hu, Xinyang Lu, Yifei Li, Jie Fu, Junxian He, Bryan Hooi
Research Question: How well can LLMs verbalize confidence, and how does verbalized confidence compare to logit and consistency metrics?
Main Method: Evaluates verbalized confidence (numerical and linguistic) mapped to calibrated probabilities across diverse models and tasks.
Datasets / Benchmarks: GSM8K, SVAMP, StrategyQA, CommonsenseQA across GPT-4, LLaMA-2
Baselines: Raw logits, length heuristics, uncalibrated verbalized confidence
Evaluation Metrics: ECE, Brier score, AUROC for failure prediction
Main Reported Findings: Verbalized confidence with lightweight calibration achieves competitive calibration to logit-based methods with near-zero overhead.
Stated Limitations: Verbalized confidence degrades on out-of-domain tasks and is sensitive to prompt phrasing.
Relationship to ThinkOrQuit: Justifies using verbalized confidence and consistency as lightweight inference features in ThinkOrQuit without requiring full model log-probabilities.
